以状态正确且内容足够的页面结果计量，不能把短输出当合格。[Q04](#research-q04)
建议观察；先在隔离宿主准备已审引擎并设严格TLS，核对公开页面与退出；敏感登录、共享宿主和高可信取证应暂缓。[Q06](#research-q06)

| 效果项 | 当前证据支持 | 尚不能确定 |

研究问题与完整回答 **插件研究总目标**：固定版本Moli适配器在哪些网页任务中优于普通fetch，认证、进程和引擎依赖是否限制采用？ ### Q01 · 本插件相对web_fetch和直接运行Moli，实际增加了什么？ **研究主题**：场景与需求、贡献与相对优势 #### 完整回答 目标是已有 DSH、需要读取 JavaScript 渲染页或保存截图的用户。普通 web_fetch 已能取得静态正文时，引入独立浏览器没有必要；动态页面、选择器容器和图片才是明确适用场景。源码注册 moli_fetch 与 moli_probe，将 Moli CLI 的渲染、选择器、文件输出及探测接入模型工具协议，合格结果是目标页面状态正确、所选内容足够且输出文件对应当前页面。浏览器渲染本身属于 Moli 上游，本插件的贡献是输入输出适配、参数冲突处理和可解释失败，而不是原创浏览器或已证明的网页准确率。作者列举的字符压缩样本只是特定页面报告，不能推出普遍节省。 #### 证据与依据 **依据 1 · 作者声明**：[README.md:13-36](https://github.com/27painter/dsh-moli/blob/56a28721fc2977f450d3ada9f03acad50e9b97d4/README.md#L13-L36) 作者给出静态fetch基线与适用任务。
查看原文（24行） ```text ## What it does, and when you want it A plain HTTP fetch returns the HTML the server sent. That is enough for articles, docs and APIs, and DSH already covers it with `web_fetch`. It is not enough for anything a browser has to build: - **Single-page apps** — a client-rendered news site, dashboard or docs site. The response is an empty shell; the content appears only after scripts run. - **Logins and consent walls** — a page that needs a session or cookie before it shows anything. - **Pictures** — a screenshot to see what a page looks like, or a PDF to keep. - **One value from deep inside a page** — a price, a count, a title, read with a selector instead of pulling the whole document. - **A list you can read for 7% of the page** — `selector` returns only the matched containers, which on a real feed measured 1,779 characters against 139,338 for the same page as Markdown. If you are about to fetch a listing page and skim it, read the `selector` section under Usage first. For those jobs this plugin gives the agent two tools: | Tool | What it does | |---|---| | `moli_fetch` | Renders a URL and returns Markdown, HTML, a semantic tree, or a JSON envelope carrying the HTTP status; **reads one container with `selector`**; evaluates a JavaScript expression; writes a PNG screenshot or a PDF | | `moli_probe` | Reports whether the engine is installed, which version, and whether HTTPS works — and installs Moli when it is missing | The practical question is whether the agent needs the page as a **browser** would see it. If a plain fetch already returns the text you want, `web_fetch` is lighter and faster. ```
**依据 2 · 源码核查**：[index.js:351-359](https://github.com/27painter/dsh-moli/blob/56a28721fc2977f450d3ada9f03acad50e9b97d4/index.js#L351-L359) 源码明确注册抓取工具及返回类型。 ```text ctx.tools.register({ name: 'moli_fetch', description: 'Fetch a URL with the local Moli headless browser: rendered HTML or Markdown, the semantic' + ' tree, a JSON envelope with status and final_url, a JavaScript expression result, a PNG screenshot, or a' + ' PDF. Use it for pages that need real rendering or JavaScript; prefer web_fetch for plain text. Screenshot' + ' and pdf dumps require writeTo. If moli is missing, run moli_probe with action "install" first.', parameters: FETCH_PARAMETERS, output: { schema: FETCH_OUTPUT_SCHEMA, render: renderFetch }, isConcurrencySafe: args => args.writeTo === undefined || args.writeTo === '', ``` ### Q02 · 选择器、滚动和输出如何保持不被静默忽略？ **研究主题**：功能与机制、工程质量与复用 #### 完整回答 moli_fetch 先定位引擎，再把参数交给 runFetch。runFetch 明确拒绝 selector 与 dump 或 eval 同用，二进制输出缺 writeTo 也拒绝，避免表面调用成功却得到另一类结果。combineEval 把滚动与选择器读取整合进单一表达式，因为上游只接受一个 --eval。抓取把stdout写文件描述符，保留二进制字节，错误页面有状态分支；空输出且无stderr可为合法空页面，有stderr则作为失败。可借鉴处是把上游CLI语义冲突转为结构化错误并让用户看见，不是只转发参数。限制是这些检查依赖Moli当前协议，不能保证未来引擎语义或所有网站行为。 #### 证据与依据 **依据 1 · 源码核查**：[lib/moli.js:148-192](https://github.com/27painter/dsh-moli/blob/56a28721fc2977f450d3ada9f03acad50e9b97d4/lib/moli.js#L148-L192) 单eval约束与滚动/读取组合。
查看原文（45行） ```text * Build the one expression the engine will run from `scroll`, `selector` and `eval`. * * The engine accepts a single `--eval`, so everything that has to happen before the * page is captured is composed here, in the order the caller expects: scroll first, * then read (a selector or the caller's expression). * * What gets returned depends on whether anything else will produce the output, and * getting this wrong breaks the feature in one direction or the other: * * - **A `dump` was requested.** The dump produces the output, so the expression is * there only for its side effects and its value is discarded by the engine anyway. * It must still be passed, or the scroll never runs. * - **No `dump`.** The expression's value *is* the output, whether it is a selector * or the caller's own expression. * - **No `dump`, no selector, no caller expression, only `scroll`.** The engine * prints whatever `--eval` evaluates to, so passing the scroll expression here * would replace the page with the scroll's return value. `undefined` is returned * instead, leaving the engine's default output -- the serialized document -- * intact. This is the case that shipped broken: `moli_fetch url=... scroll=600` * answered `600`. * * @param evalExpression - the caller's expression, if any. * @param scroll - the caller's `scroll` value, if any. * @param hasDump - whether the caller also asked for a dump. * @param selector - the caller's CSS selector, if any. * @returns the expression to pass, or undefined to let the engine decide. */ export function combineEval(evalExpression, scroll, hasDump = false, selector = undefined) { const move = scrollScript(scroll); const read = selectorScript(selector); const caller = evalExpression === undefined || evalExpression === '' ? undefined : evalExpression; // A selector is a read, so it replaces the caller's expression rather than being // chained with it; `buildArgs` rejects the two together, so only one is ever set. // The selector script is already a call expression; a caller's expression has to be // wrapped so its value is what the engine reports. const body = read !== undefined ? { code: read, wrapped: true } : (caller === undefined ? undefined : { code: caller, wrapped: false }); if (move === undefined) return body === undefined ? undefined : body.code; if (body === undefined) { // No read at all: keep the scroll only when a dump will produce the output. return hasDump ? move : undefined; } // The read goes last so its value is the one the engine reports; losing it would // contradict the documented `eval` behaviour. ```

'pdf' : 'png'} path, then read that file.`, }; ```

      "path": "README.md",
      "content": "# dsh-moli

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/dsh-moli)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-moli)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/dsh-moli)](LICENSE)
[![listed in awesome-dsh-plugin](https://img.shields.io/badge/awesome--dsh--plugin-listed-3964fe)](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin)

**Two tools that let a DeepSeek Harness agent drive a real headless browser.** They wrap
[Moli](https://github.com/lexmount/moli) — a Rust headless browser built for AI agents — so an agent can
read pages that only exist after JavaScript runs, and can produce pictures of them.

English | [中文](README.zh.md)

## What it does, and when you want it

A plain HTTP fetch returns the HTML the server sent. That is enough for articles, docs and APIs, and
DSH already covers it with `web_fetch`. It is not enough for anything a browser has to build:

- **Single-page apps** — a client-rendered news site, dashboard or docs site. The response is an empty
  shell; the content appears only after scripts run.
- **Logins and consent walls** — a page that needs a session or cookie before it shows anything.
- **Pictures** — a screenshot to see what a page looks like, or a PDF to keep.
- **One value from deep inside a page** — a price, a count, a title, read with a selector instead of
  pulling the whole document.
- **A list you can read for 7% of the page** — `selector` returns only the matched containers, which
  on a real feed measured 1,779 characters against 139,338 for the same page as Markdown. If you are
  about to fetch a listing page and skim it, read the `selector` section under Usage first.

For those jobs this plugin gives the agent two tools:

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `moli_fetch` | Renders a URL and returns Markdown, HTML, a semantic tree, or a JSON envelope carrying the HTTP status; **reads one container with `selector`**; evaluates a JavaScript expression; writes a PNG screenshot or a PDF |
| `moli_probe` | Reports whether the engine is installed, which version, and whether HTTPS works — and installs Moli when it is missing |

The practical question is whether the agent needs the page as a **browser** would see it. If a plain
fetch already returns the text you want, `web_fetch` is lighter and faster.

```
  agent ──moli_fetch──▶ dsh-moli plugin ──spawns──▶ moli.exe
                              ▲                         │
                              │                    renders the page,
                              │                    runs its JavaScript
                              │                         │
                              └──markdown / json / png / pdf◀┘
```

## Install

Two routes. Both install the same plugin; pick by what your network reaches.

**Route 1 — from npm (recommended).** Resolves through the npm registry, so it works where GitHub is
slow or blocked, and DSH's install dialog can fall back to a regional mirror:

```powershell
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-moli
```

**Route 2 — straight from the repository.** Tracks the source directly; needs GitHub to be reachable:

```powershell
dsh plugin --profile web add github:27painter/dsh-moli
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The npm package is the plugin only — it does not contain the Moli engine.**
>
> The npm tarball is 26 kB: eight JavaScript and text files. `moli.exe` is a separate ~101 MB compiled
> Rust binary, built and released by the Moli project on its own schedule.
>
> **Why it cannot be bundled:**
>
> - **Size.** The engine is roughly 4,000× the plugin. Every install and every plugin update would
>   carry a browser.
> - **Ownership.** Moli is `lexmount/moli` under its own MIT copyright. Redistributing its binary
>   through this package would mean re-publishing someone else's artifact as our own.
> - **Platforms.** The engine ships per OS and per architecture — Windows/Linux/macOS × x64/arm64.
>   Bundling would pin one build into every user's install.
> - **Versions.** The plugin must work with whatever Moli version a user has, including Moli releases
>   that appear after the plugin was published. Bundling would lock the pair together.
>
> **There is no npm package for the engine either.** The registry names `moli` and `moli-cli` belong to
> unrelated projects, and `@lexmount/moli` does not exist. Moli ships as prebuilt binaries on
> [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/lexmount/moli/releases/latest) — do not install the engine by
> guessing a package name.

## The two situations after installing

The two download routes above install the same thing. What differs is whether Moli is already on the
machine — and that decides whether you are finished or have one more step.

### Situation A — Moli is already installed: nothing else to do

The plugin discovers `moli.exe` on its own and both tools work immediately. Just restart DSH and
confirm:

```
moli_probe
```

If the reported version looks right, you are done.

### Situation B — Moli is not installed yet: fetch the engine too

`moli_fetch` will keep reporting a missing engine until you install one. Do that with either of:

```
moli_probe action=install          # let the plugin fetch it
```

```powershell
# or run Moli's own installer yourself
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://github.com/lexmount/moli/releases/latest/download/moli-installer.ps1 | iex"
```

Then confirm with `moli_probe` and fetch a page:

```
moli_probe
moli_fetch url=https://example.com dump=markdown
```

### Getting the Moli engine

`moli_probe` reports whether the engine is present. If it is not, pick one of:

**1. Let the plugin install it** — tries several download routes and reports a SHA256 of what it ran.
   The whole run is asynchronous (the host keeps serving), and a configured `proxy` is passed to both
   the download routes and the installer's own engine download:

```
moli_probe action=install
```

**2. Official one-line installer** (Moli's own documented commands):

```powershell
# Windows
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://github.com/lexmount/moli/releases/latest/download/moli-installer.ps1 | iex"
```

```sh
# Linux / macOS
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://github.com/lexmount/moli/releases/latest/download/moli-installer.sh | sh
```

**3. Direct binary,** if you would rather not run an installer:

```powershell
# pick the asset matching your architecture from the releases page
curl.exe -L -o moli.zip https://github.com/lexmount/moli/releases/latest/download/moli-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip
Expand-Archive moli.zip -DestinationPath "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Moli" -Force
```

Those `releases/latest/download/...` URLs always resolve to the newest release, so they stay valid
without pinning a version.

After any of them, point the plugin at the result if it landed somewhere unusual:

```yaml
config:
  exePath: 'C:\path\to\moli.exe'
```

#### Verifying the download

Moli's README documents no checksum or signature, and the installer publishes no checksum file. What
does exist is GitHub's own per-asset `sha256` digest, readable from the release API:

```powershell
(irm https://api.github.com/repos/lexmount/moli/releases/latest).assets | Select-Object name, digest
```

For `v1.1.17` that reports, among others:

```
moli-installer.ps1                2,020  sha256:e002f7a6c174d78ae6ed7289aca9f5d3a62ab0b1f6e588606a80c0cb5d37964d
moli-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip  43.8 MB  sha256:5247309837b6eaf6e73bfa18f2a8d8d90473b9e2fe5cfcaaef57d7eee9b074c4
```

Compare it against the file you downloaded:

```powershell
(Get-FileHash .\moli-installer.ps1 -Algorithm SHA256).Hash.ToLower()
```

The plugin follows the same discipline: `moli_probe action=install` reports the SHA256 of the bytes it
ran, and `expectedSha256` turns that report into an enforced gate. It does not invent a trusted
default, because a digest only means something when compared against the release page's own value.

This is a checked property rather than a claim: downloading `v1.1.17`'s installer through the plugin's
own `downloadInstaller` reproduced `e002f7a6…964d` exactly — the digest GitHub publishes — and
re-hashing the file from disk matched as well.

### Installing into a desktop profile

`dsh plugin --profile desktop …` is refused — the desktop profile belongs to the Electron app. Either
edit its `package.json` directly, or use the in-app plugin page (sidebar → **Plugins** → **Add
plugin**), which installs through the same pnpm path.

A profile plugin needs both halves: a dependency edge (`dependencies`) and a
`dsh.profile.bundles` entry. One without the other leaves the plugin invisible to the loader. From a
local checkout the four steps are:

1. Put this directory anywhere, e.g. `D:\dsh_plugins\dsh-moli`.
2. Add both entries to the profile's `package.json`:
   - `dependencies`: `"dsh-moli": "link:D:/dsh_plugins/dsh-moli"`
   - `dsh.profile.bundles`: `"dsh-moli"`
3. Run `pnpm install` in the profile directory (creates `node_modules/dsh-moli`).
4. Restart DSH.

An unresolvable bundle is **skipped silently** apart from one stderr line
(`skipping profile bundle …`). If the tools never appear, that line is the first thing to look for.

## Usage

`moli_fetch` parameters: `url` (required), `dump`, `writeTo`, `selector`, `eval`, `scroll`, `wait`,
`waitSelector`, `waitScript`, `waitResponseUrl`, `waitResponseJson`, `delayMs`, `timeoutMs`,
`maxChars`, `headers`, `userAgent`, `layout`, `scrollbars`, `noJs`, `noCss`, `resources`,
`withFrames`, `insecureTls`, `failOnHttpError`, `profileDir`, `cookieFile`, `proxy`.

```
moli_fetch url=https://example.com dump=markdown             # token-efficient text
moli_fetch url=https://example.com dump=semantic_tree_text    # nodes with backend ids
moli_fetch url=https://example.com eval="document.title"      # one computed value
moli_fetch url=https://example.com selector=".video-card"     # one container, not the page
moli_fetch url=https://example.com dump=screenshot writeTo=/abs/path/a.png
moli_fetch url=https://example.com dump=pdf        writeTo=/abs/path/a.pdf
moli_fetch url=https://example.com dump=markdown scroll=800   # trigger lazy loading first
```

Screenshot and PDF dumps need `writeTo`; the bytes are written verbatim rather than printed.

### `selector` — pay for the items, not the page

**This is the cheapest way to read a page with this plugin, and usually the one you want.**

A listing page is mostly noise if you only want the items. `selector` returns the text of
the elements a CSS selector matches, so you pay for the part you asked for instead of for
the whole document. Measured on the same page, same moment:

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `dump=markdown` | 139,338 characters |
| `selector=".bili-video-card"` | 1,779 characters, 47 matches |

**78x less to read** — and the difference is not just cost. The full page arrives with
navigation, footers, cookie banners and recommendation rails; the selector result is the
47 rows you asked for, with nothing to sift out afterwards.

```
moli_fetch url=https://example.com/feed selector=".video-card"
moli_fetch url=https://example.com/feed selector="h2" scroll=2000    # scroll first, then read
moli_fetch url="https://www.bing.com/search?q=deepseek+harness" selector=".b_algo"
```

That last one is worth pointing out: **a search engine's results page is just a page**, so
one fetch plus one selector reads it, with no search API and no per-query cost. It is also
why the plugin still exposes only `fetch` — searching is a selector call, not a separate
tool. Engines block clients at different rates, so if one refuses the request, try another.

All matches are joined with newlines and the result reports how many there were:
"matched 48 element(s)" is the difference between a complete read and a partial one,
and it is the only signal you get that the selector was too broad or too narrow.

Two cases are deliberately errors rather than empty answers, because the engine
cannot tell an empty selection from a page with no text — an expression returning
`""` exits 0 with a blank line:

- **nothing matched** — `ok: false`, "no element matches". A selector that is not on
  the page is almost always a spelling mistake or a page that has not loaded yet.
- **matched, but no text** — `ok: false`, "match but none of them has any text", which
  is what an icon or an image container gives you. Use `eval` if you need attributes.

`selector` cannot be combined with `dump` or `eval`: a selector returns one
container's text, a dump returns the whole page, and only one expression value can be
returned — so one of them could only be silently ignored, which is the failure mode
this plugin keeps having to fix.

### `scroll` — reach what only appears on a scroll

The engine serializes the whole document, so a plain fetch already contains everything the DOM holds.
What it cannot contain is content that does not exist yet: a list that loads on the first `scroll`
event, an `IntersectionObserver` that fires on entry, an image swapped in when it nears the viewport.
`scroll` runs the scroll before the capture, so those handlers fire first.

```
moli_fetch url=https://example.com/feed dump=markdown scroll=600
moli_fetch url=https://example.com/feed dump=markdown scroll=bottom
moli_fetch url=https://example.com/feed dump=markdown scroll=-400    # back up
```

Measured on a page whose `scroll` handler fills a slot: without `scroll` the dump says
`STILL-EMPTY`, with `scroll=1000` it says `LAZY-CONTENT-1000`. It also moves the screenshot, so a
scrolled `dump=screenshot` shows that part of the page.

`scroll` is a side effect, so it composes and stands alone:

```
moli_fetch url=... dump=markdown scroll=600      # scroll, then dump the page
moli_fetch url=... eval="document.title" scroll=600   # scroll, then read a value
moli_fetch url=... scroll=600                    # just scroll; you still get the page
```

The last form is worth spelling out because it was broken. The scroll runs in the engine's own
pre-capture evaluation, and without `dump` the engine prints whatever that evaluation returns — so an
earlier version that returned the scroll position made this call answer `600` instead of the document,
while the identical call without `scroll` returned 1,989 characters of HTML. A scroll reports nothing
now; it only happens.

### `eval` with `dump` — the expression value is dropped

The engine documents this and it is kept, because using an expression to change a page before
capturing it is a real pattern. What is not acceptable is that it used to look like a clean answer:
`eval='JSON.stringify({probe:1})'` with `dump=markdown` returned 900 characters of Markdown, reported
`ok: true`, and said nothing. The result now carries `evalDiscarded: true` and a note, and the rendered
output leads with the warning rather than burying it under the body.

If you want the expression's value, pass `eval` without `dump`.

### `failOnHttpError` — stop reading an error page as content

By default a 404 is returned like any other page, so a failed fetch looks successful. Setting
`failOnHttpError` turns a final status of 400 or above into `ok: false` with the status named — and
**keeps the body**, because an error page is often the thing you need to read.

```
moli_fetch url=https://example.com/nope dump=markdown failOnHttpError=true
```

| | default | `failOnHttpError: true` |
|---|---|---|
| a 404 | `ok: true`, the error page as content | `ok: false`, `status: 404`, body still returned |
| a screenshot of a 404 | written as a normal image | still written, and reported as a failure |

It is off by default so existing calls keep their behaviour. A JSON dump already reported the status
on its own; markdown and HTML dumps did not, and that is the gap this closes.

### Waiting for what the page actually fetches

`wait: "networkidle"` plus `delayMs` is a guess about how long a list takes to arrive. These wait for
the request itself:

```
# the response that carries the data
moli_fetch url=https://example.com/feed dump=markdown waitResponseUrl="/api/feed"

# the payload, when the URL is not distinctive
moli_fetch url=https://example.com/feed dump=markdown waitResponseJson="data.list.0.id=42"

# the page's own idea of readiness
moli_fetch url=https://example.com/app dump=markdown waitScript="window.appReady === true"
```

`waitResponseJson` takes `PATH=VALUE`, where `PATH` addresses the field and `VALUE` is compared
literally. Use these when a fixed delay either wastes time or reads the page too early.

## Relationship to Moli's own agent skills

Moli ships official agent skills in its repository — [`moli-webfetch`](https://github.com/lexmount/moli/tree/main/skills/moli-webfetch),
[`moli-websearch`](https://github.com/lexmount/moli/tree/main/skills/moli-websearch), and
[`moli-cdp-server`](https://github.com/lexmount/moli/tree/main/skills/moli-cdp-server) — and their
README's quick start is to have an agent install them. If your agent loads skills, the simplest path
is to point it at those; they are maintained upstream and cover web search and a CDP server too.

This plugin exists because it is a different trade-off, not a replacement:

- **Always-on tool schemas instead of an on-demand skill.** The tools are registered at Host startup,
  so the model sees them every turn with no discovery step.
- **DSH-specific failure handling.** The three traps below (sandbox pipe capture, UTF-16 mangling of
  binary output, bare-specifier resolution for a `link:`ed plugin) plus sandbox/revocation/proxy
  classification are solved here, because they are DSH-on-Windows problems.
- **Smaller surface.** Only `fetch` is wrapped; the official skills also cover web search and the CDP
  server, which this plugin does not.

Both can coexist: install the skills if you want upstream coverage, keep this plugin if you want the
capabilities always visible to the model.

## Three design points

1. **Output goes through file descriptors, never pipes.** Under DSH's Windows sandbox a child
   process cannot open an inherited named pipe, so `spawnSync(..., { stdio: 'pipe' })` returns
   `status=null` and zero bytes. Every run redirects stdout/stderr to real files and reads them back.
2. **Binary output is copied byte for byte.** PowerShell's `>` operator re-encodes a native
   program's output as UTF-16, inserting a `00` after every byte, which corrupts a screenshot.
   Bytes here are written verbatim, so the PNG signature stays `89504e470d0a1a0a`.
3. **One optional external dependency.** A profile plugin is loaded from its real path on disk (a `link:`
   dependency stays a symlink target), so a bare specifier such as `@deepseek-ai/schemastery`
   resolves against the plugin directory instead of the profile's `node_modules`. The import is
   therefore guarded: without schemastery (a `link:` install) the settings form does not appear and
   the plugin degrades to plain patch-layer configuration, while `moli_fetch` and `moli_probe` keep
   registering. With it (a normal npm install, which brings the dependency along) the settings page
   is available.

## Platform support

Works on **Windows, Linux and macOS** (x64 / arm64).

> **Linux and macOS support was contributed by [@nd002723](https://github.com/nd002723)** in
> [PR #1](https://github.com/27painter/dsh-moli/pull/1): engine discovery in the standard POSIX
> locations, the `sh` installer route, and the per-platform gating of the PowerShell paths.

| Platform | Status |
|---|---|
| **Windows** | Verified by the maintainer |
| **Linux** | Verified by the contributor, not the maintainer: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, Node v24.21.0, Moli 1.1.17 — including the async install path, proxy injection, and a `strace`-recorded end-to-end fetch |
| **macOS** | Verified in CI, not on a personal Mac: `macos-latest` (Apple Silicon, arm64) with a real Moli 1.1.19 engine downloaded from the official release. The plugin found it at `~/.local/bin/moli`, rendered pages, and the `scroll` and `selector` end-to-end halves passed instead of skipping |

- **Windows** — the engine is located at the official installer paths (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Moli\bin\moli.exe`,
  `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin\moli.exe`) with a recursive scan of `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Moli` as a fallback.
  `moli_probe action=install` runs the official PowerShell installer.
- **Linux / macOS** — the engine is found in the standard locations (`~/.local/bin/moli`,
  `~/.local/share/moli/bin/moli`, `~/.local/share/moli/moli`, `~/.moli/bin/moli`) and on `$PATH`.
  `moli_probe action=install` runs the official `moli-installer.sh` via `sh`.

**Installing never blocks the DSH host.** Both the installer download and the execution of the
official installer spawn asynchronously with a timeout that escalates from SIGTERM to SIGKILL, and
an interrupted turn aborts the child immediately — the host keeps serving while Moli's installer
does its work. A `strace -e trace=connect` run against a real install recorded every connection
going through the configured proxy port and none to the upstream host, and a fixture installer
confirmed the proxy arrives in the child's environment.

The configured `proxy` feeds **both** phases: the plugin's own download routes (`curl --proxy`, and
`-Proxy` on PowerShell's `Invoke-WebRequest`), and the official installer's internal engine download
— on Windows through a `DefaultWebProxy` prelude (PowerShell's `Invoke-WebRequest` ignores proxy
environment variables), on POSIX through the standard `HTTPS_PROXY`/`HTTP_PROXY`/`ALL_PROXY`
variables the installer's `curl` reads. A proxy carrying credentials sets them explicitly.

On Linux, `moli_probe` discovered `~/.local/bin/moli` unaided, and `moli_fetch` rendered a
region-gated storefront end to end — through a local forward proxy, with a Netscape `cookieFile` —
returning a 500+ KB page whose final URL carried the cookie-driven query parameters. That run
exercised the proxy download route as well as the engine paths.

## Configuration

Override any field under the plugin's `config` entry in the profile patch layer. All are optional.
The same fields are also editable from the **Moli 安装与抓取** settings section on the plugin's page in
the Plugins manager (a `plugins.bundle.config` form registered by the browser half).

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: dsh-moli
      name: dsh-moli
      config:
        exePath: 'C:\Users\me\AppData\Local\Moli\bin\moli.exe'  # default: auto-detect
        defaultTimeoutMs: 30000                                  # per-fetch readiness deadline
        maxChars: 200000                                         # inline text truncation
        proxy: 'http://127.0.0.1:7890'                           # forward proxy for moli, downloads, and the installer's engine download
        insecureTls: true                                        # see the TLS notes below
```

The plugin-level `proxy` above is the default; `moli_fetch` also takes a `proxy` argument, so a single
call can route through a different proxy without changing the profile. A loopback URL always bypasses
whichever proxy is in effect.

Without `exePath`, the plugin probes `exePath` → `MOLI_BIN` → `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Moli\bin\moli.exe` →
`%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin\moli.exe`, then scans inside `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Moli` for a `moli.exe`, so an
installation under a versioned subdirectory is still found.

### Engine lifecycle from the settings page

The settings section also carries an **engine** row that detects the installed engine and lets you
install or uninstall it without touching the profile:

- **state** — `engineState` is `installed` (with `engineVersion`), `missing`, or a short error text.
- **install** — the form writes `engineAction: "install"`; the host downloads and runs the official
  installer asynchronously, then reports the outcome back through `engineState` / `engineVersion`.
- **uninstall** — `engineAction: "uninstall"` removes the engine. On Windows only the installer-owned
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Moli` tree is deleted; without one, nothing is touched. On POSIX the located binary
  is removed and the now-empty install directories are pruned.

These three fields (`engineAction`, `engineState`, `engineVersion`) are part of the live Config schema;
`engineAction` is a `none`/`install`/`uninstall` union. They are meant to be driven by the settings
form, so prefer editing the four fields above for routine configuration.

## Known limitations

- **The Linux and macOS paths were written, and the maintainer's own hardware cannot run them.** The
  maintainer is a student with no macOS or Linux machine, so engine discovery at the POSIX locations
  and the `sh` installer route came from [@nd002723](https://github.com/nd002723). Linux was verified
  by them on Ubuntu 24.04; macOS is now covered by CI, which installs the official darwin build and
  runs the page-level suites on `macos-latest` (Apple Silicon, arm64) — see
  [Platform support](#platform-support) for exactly what that exercised. **A CI runner is not a
  desktop, so if something fails on either platform, please open an
  [issue](https://github.com/27painter/dsh-moli/issues) with the error output** — that is still the
  only way the paths users actually take get fixed.
- **Moli itself is not bundled.** Install it separately or let `moli_probe action=install` fetch it.
- **Only `fetch` is wrapped.** `moli serve` (CDP/WebDriver server) and `moli import` (session
  import) are not exposed as tools yet.
- **No per-call cancellation for fetches.** The engine runs synchronously for a fetch, so an
  interrupted turn cannot abort it mid-flight; a call already in progress finishes and its artifact
  is written. `moli_probe action=install` is the exception — it is asynchronous and aborts the child
  immediately on an interrupted turn.
- **HTTP error status is only visible for `dump: json`.** That is the only dump format carrying the
  status field. With `markdown` or `html` an error page is returned as content.
- **`writeTo` calls are serialized.** They report as unsafe to parallelize, so two artifact writes
  never interleave.
- **`insecureTls` defaults to `true`.** Behind a filtering proxy the certificate-revocation
  responder is often unreachable, and Schannel then fails with
  `CRYPT_E_REVOCATION_OFFLINE (0x80092013)` on hosts like GitHub. The default passes moli's
  `--insecure-disable-tls-host-verification`. Set `insecureTls: false` on networks where revocation
  checks work, or per call with `insecureTls: false`.
- **Sandbox interaction.** Under DSH's default file sandbox, a subprocess runs at low integrity and
  Schannel cannot acquire client credentials, so HTTPS fails with `SEC_E_NO_CREDENTIALS`. Plain
  HTTP still works and the failure is reported structurally (`sandboxTlsBlock: true`) with the
  retry path; passing `sandbox_permissions: "danger-full-access"` for that call resolves it.
- **Host reachability varies on some networks.** Observed on the development machine: `curl`-based
  clients (Moli) timed out on `github.com` while `git` over HTTPS and the system browser reached it
  in seconds, and `api.github.com` worked where `github.com` did not — at the same moment. Treat a
  timeout as possibly transient: retry, or set `proxy`. Because a bare timeout is ambiguous, it is
  reported as `possiblyUnreachable` rather than a verdict. The install action's multi-route fallback
  and the manual commands above exist for exactly this case.

## Verification

Eight suites live in [`verify/`](verify/), and all are runnable against a working tree:

CI runs them on three operating systems, in two tiers. The **core** tier runs on Ubuntu, Windows
and macOS and needs no engine; its end-to-end halves use `data:` URLs and skip when no engine is
present. The **engine** tier runs on all three as well, but there it *downloads a real Moli
release first* and treats a skip as a failure — otherwise "the tests passed" would only mean "the
code loaded". That is what backs the macOS row in [Platform support](#platform-support): the
plugin found the engine, rendered pages, and the `scroll` and `selector` page halves executed.

- `config-verify.mjs` checks the settings surface and engine lifecycle added by the plugin's browser
  half: the volatile `Config` schema (every declared field, `engineAction` as a `none`/`install`/
  `uninstall` union), `apply` reading both a plain config and a volatile `.get()` reference, the
  `settings/document-updated` wiring, `uninstallMoli` (platform-aware: POSIX removes the located
  binary, Windows removes only the installer-owned `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Moli` tree), and the client.js
  shape (`plugins.bundle.config` registration, zh/en dictionaries, raw `true`/`false` select labels).
- `schema-verify.mjs` checks the tool definitions with the registry's own validator, including
  controls that assert the two invalid schema shapes still fail.
- `install-verify.mjs` drives the install pipeline against a loopback HTTP server: route ordering,
  the SHA256 of served bytes, refusal to execute on a checksum mismatch, actual execution when the
  digest matches, and the all-routes-failed diagnostic.
- `linux-verify.mjs` (POSIX hosts) asserts the proxy-helper functions, then against a real install
  proves the two guarantees of the async rewrite: the installer child actually receives the proxy
  through its environment (`HTTPS_PROXY` captured by a fixture installer), and the host event loop
  stays live while a slow installer runs — the acceptance criterion for the async path.
- `win-verify.mjs` (Windows hosts) runs the same pure assertions, then executes the `DefaultWebProxy`
  prelude in a real `powershell.exe` and inspects the proxy object and credentials it set, exercises
  the Windows download routes, and runs `installMoli` end to end.
- `empty-verify.mjs` asserts, against three compiled stub engines, that a fetch which exits 0 with no
  output is a successful empty result rather than an error, that a non-zero exit still fails, and that
  a complaint on stderr with no stdout is not mistaken for an empty page.
- `report-verify.mjs` guards the findings from a usage report: `eval` documents that pairing it with
  `dump` discards its value, an expression that throws is classified as such instead of being blamed
  on the installation, truncation keeps the tail as well as the head, `proxy` is a per-call parameter,
  and `moli_probe` states which process its `httpsOk` describes.
- `scroll-verify.mjs` checks the expression builder without an engine (pixels, negatives, `top`,
  `bottom`, nonsense rejected, the caller's `eval` value preserved) and then, when an engine is
  present, fetches a page whose `scroll` handler fills a slot and asserts the content appears with
  `scroll` and the placeholder appears without it — a property of the output, not of an internal call.
- `selector-verify.mjs` covers the two silent-wrong-answer cases a container read invites: a selector
  matching nothing is an error rather than empty content, and a selector matching several elements
  reports the count and joins them. It also asserts that the selector is quoted as data rather than
  spliced into the expression, that `selector` with `dump` or `eval` is refused instead of one of them
  being ignored, and that it composes with `scroll`.
- `http-verify.mjs` asserts the parameter-to-flag mapping directly, because a parameter that never
  reaches the engine is indistinguishable from a feature that does not work. It then fetches a 404 and
  checks that `failOnHttpError` reports it while keeping the body, that a healthy page is unaffected,
  and that a screenshot of an error page is still written as a valid PNG rather than decoded as text.
  It also covers the two silent-answer cases: `eval` with `dump` is flagged `evalDiscarded` and the
  warning renders first, and `scroll` alone returns the document rather than the scroll offset.
  The end-to-end half needs an HTTP error from a real server: loopback is unreachable from inside this
  sandbox — `curl.exe` times out on `127.0.0.1` while the Node host reaches it — so it uses a path
  under `example.com` and skips when the network is away.

`.github/workflows/verify.yml` runs `schema-verify`, `empty-verify`, `config-verify`, `scroll-verify`,
`selector-verify`, `http-verify` and `link-install-verify` on Linux, Windows and macOS — the core
tier, which needs no engine and no network. A second tier runs the engine-dependent suites on all
three as well, and installs a real Moli release on macOS first, treating a missing engine as a skip
there only where the suite is platform-specific.

`report-verify.mjs` is deliberately **not** in CI. Three of its checks fetch `example.com` and one
fetches a specific forum thread, so it needs the open internet — and on a host whose traffic goes
through a proxy, that proxy too. Useful where a network is available, but a suite that goes red
because a website changed is worse than no suite, so it stays a local check. If you run it and see
failures in sections 4–6 while sections 1–3 pass, suspect the network before the code.

### Prerequisites for the suites

The plugin has one optional runtime dependency — [`@deepseek-ai/schemastery`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@deepseek-ai/schemastery) — used by the live `Config` schema that registers the settings namespace (optional because the import is guarded, so a `link:` install without it still loads and registers the tools). Suites that import the plugin (`config-verify`, `schema-verify`, `empty-verify`, `report-verify`, `http-verify`) need it resolvable from the working tree, so run `npm install` first.

`schema-verify` additionally imports the registry's own validator out of the npm-global `@deepseek-ai/dsh` install (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools`); `report-verify` and the engine suites need a real Moli engine, and `empty-verify` needs a C compiler to build its stub engines. On Windows, `@deepseek-ai/schemastery` can be resolved through a directory junction into the fork's `node_modules` from the npm-global DSH tree, the same way the suites resolve `dsh-tools`.

Beyond those, `lib/moli.js` and the tool layer were exercised end to end against Moli 1.1.16 on
Windows: registration, probe, Markdown and JSON dumps, `eval` (including a tight-timeout regression
guard for the `-t` argument position), PNG and PDF artifacts with valid signatures, truncation, every
rejection path (binary dump without `writeTo`, unknown `dump`, unknown `wait` stage, missing
destination directory), failure classification (unreachable host, HTTP status, sandbox TLS block,
revocation block), and the concurrency claims. The blocked-host classifier is covered by pure
function tests using stderr text captured from real runs.

Confirmed at runtime too: a JavaScript-rendered page (GitHub search) returned 14,560 characters of
Markdown containing 30 real repository matches when fetched through a local proxy. A throwaway
profile with the plugin installed composes its config with no `JsonSchemaError` and no skipped bundle.

 * wrong, which is what a model that is not fluent in the DOM needs.
 *
 * It works within one navigation -- the value is returned by the engine's own
 * evaluation, so the "page is gone by the time the result is assembled" limitation
 * does not apply.
 *
 * The result is prefixed with a machine-readable count, because the engine prints an
 * empty string for an expression that yields `""`, and an empty selection is
 * otherwise indistinguishable from a page with no text. A selector that matches
 * nothing is reported as a failure rather than as empty content: the caller picked a
 * selector that is not on the page, and telling them so is the whole point.
 *
 * @param selector - a CSS selector.
 * @returns a JavaScript expression, or undefined when no selector was given.
 */
export function selectorScript(selector) {
  if (typeof selector !== 'string' || selector.trim() === '') return undefined;
  // JSON.stringify quotes the selector safely for embedding; a selector is data, not
  // code, and must never be spliced into the expression raw.
  const quoted = JSON.stringify(selector);
  return `(() => {
    const nodes = [...document.querySelectorAll(${quoted})];
    // Fall back to textContent when innerText is EMPTY, not merely absent.
    // \`??\` treats an empty string as a value, so a page whose layout has not been
    // computed for these nodes returned "matched N but none has any text" -- measured
    // on Bing: 10 matched elements, all with an innerText of '' and a textContent of
    // 150-240 characters. That is a wrong failure for a page that reads fine.
    const texts = nodes.map(node => {
      const inner = (node.innerText ?? '').trim();
      return inner !== '' ? inner : (node.textContent ?? '').trim();
    }).filter(text => text !== '');
    return '[dsh-moli:selector]' + JSON.stringify({
      matched: nodes.length,
      withText: texts.length,
      joined: texts.join('\\n'),
    });
  })()`;
}

/**
 * Build the expression that scrolls the page, to be run by the engine's own
 * `--eval` before the dump.
 *
 * Scrolling is not a nicety: a page can load content on its first scroll event, and
 * then a fetch without scrolling sees a placeholder while the same fetch with it
 * sees the content. Verified against a page whose scroll handler fills a slot --
 * the dump carried the loaded text with `scroll` and the placeholder without it.
 * Moli does serialize the whole document either way, so this is not about reaching
 * content that "below the fold" already contains; it is about triggering the
 * handler, the intersection observer, or the lazy image that only runs on a scroll.
 *
 * **The expression must not return the scroll position.** Without `--dump` the
 * engine prints whatever `--eval` evaluates to, so returning `String(window.scrollY)`
 * here replaced the page with the number `600`: `moli_fetch url=... scroll=600`
 * answered `600`, while the identical call without `scroll` returned the document's
 * HTML. The scroll is a side effect; the value it wants to report is recorded on
 * `window` instead, where a later read can pick it up without changing what the
 * engine prints.
 *
 * @param scroll - pixels down (negative scrolls up), or `top` / `bottom`.
 * @returns a JavaScript expression, or undefined when there is nothing to do.
 */
export function scrollScript(scroll) {
  if (scroll === undefined || scroll === null) return undefined;
  let target;
  if (typeof scroll === 'number') {
    if (!Number.isFinite(scroll)) return undefined;
    target = String(Math.trunc(scroll));
  } else if (typeof scroll === 'string') {
    const key = scroll.trim().toLowerCase();
    if (key === '') return undefined;
    target = SCROLL_TOKENS[key] ?? (/^-?\d+$/u.test(key) ? key : undefined);
    if (target === undefined) return undefined;
  } else {
    return undefined;
  }
  // Dispatch a scroll event as well as moving: `window.scrollTo` updates the
  // position, but a page listening for the event is the reason this exists. The
  // height is captured on both sides of the move so a caller can tell whether the
  // page grew -- which is the one signal that says lazy loading actually happened.
  return `(() => {
    const before = document.body === null ? 0 : document.body.scrollHeight;
    window.scrollTo(0, ${target});
    window.dispatchEvent(new Event('scroll'));
    window.__dshMoliScroll = {
      requested: ${target},
      y: window.scrollY,
      heightBefore: before,
      heightAfter: document.body === null ? 0 : document.body.scrollHeight,
    };
  })()`;
}

/**
 * Build the one expression the engine will run from `scroll`, `selector` and `eval`.
 *
 * The engine accepts a single `--eval`, so everything that has to happen before the
 * page is captured is composed here, in the order the caller expects: scroll first,
 * then read (a selector or the caller's expression).
 *
 * What gets returned depends on whether anything else will produce the output, and
 * getting this wrong breaks the feature in one direction or the other:
 *
 * - **A `dump` was requested.** The dump produces the output, so the expression is
 *   there only for its side effects and its value is discarded by the engine anyway.
 *   It must still be passed, or the scroll never runs.
 * - **No `dump`.** The expression's value *is* the output, whether it is a selector
 *   or the caller's own expression.
 * - **No `dump`, no selector, no caller expression, only `scroll`.** The engine
 *   prints whatever `--eval` evaluates to, so passing the scroll expression here
 *   would replace the page with the scroll's return value. `undefined` is returned
 *   instead, leaving the engine's default output -- the serialized document --
 *   intact. This is the case that shipped broken: `moli_fetch url=... scroll=600`
 *   answered `600`.
 *
 * @param evalExpression - the caller's expression, if any.
 * @param scroll - the caller's `scroll` value, if any.
 * @param hasDump - whether the caller also asked for a dump.
 * @param selector - the caller's CSS selector, if any.
 * @returns the expression to pass, or undefined to let the engine decide.
 */
export function combineEval(evalExpression, scroll, hasDump = false, selector = undefined) {
  const move = scrollScript(scroll);
  const read = selectorScript(selector);
  const caller = evalExpression === undefined || evalExpression === '' ? undefined : evalExpression;

  // A selector is a read, so it replaces the caller's expression rather than being
  // chained with it; `buildArgs` rejects the two together, so only one is ever set.
  // The selector script is already a call expression; a caller's expression has to be
  // wrapped so its value is what the engine reports.
  const body = read !== undefined ? { code: read, wrapped: true } : (caller === undefined ? undefined : { code: caller, wrapped: false });

  if (move === undefined) return body === undefined ? undefined : body.code;
  if (body === undefined) {
    // No read at all: keep the scroll only when a dump will produce the output.
    return hasDump ? move : undefined;
  }
  // The read goes last so its value is the one the engine reports; losing it would
  // contradict the documented `eval` behaviour.
  return `${move}; ${body.wrapped ? body.code : `(() => (${body.code}))()`}`;
}

/**
 * Every place this plugin will look for `moli.exe`, most explicit first.
 *
 * The recursive `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Moli` entry exists because Moli's installer has
 * placed the binary under versioned subdirectories, so a fixed `bin\moli.exe`
 * path is not enough to find an installation that plainly exists.
 *
 * @param override - explicit path from configuration, when set.
 * @returns candidate paths, in probe order.
 */
export function moliCandidates(override) {
  const isWin = process.platform === 'win32';
  const home = process.env.HOME ?? homedir();
  const listed = [
    override,
    process.env.MOLI_BIN,
    // Windows: official installer location.
    isWin && process.env.LOCALAPPDATA !== undefined ? join(process.env.LOCALAPPDATA, 'Moli', 'bin', 'moli.exe') : undefined,
    isWin && process.env.USERPROFILE !== undefined ? join(process.env.USERPROFILE, '.local', 'bin', 'moli.exe') : undefined,
    // Linux/macOS: installer.sh default ~/.local/bin/moli, plus versioned/shared dirs.
    !isWin ? join(home, '.local', 'bin', 'moli') : undefined,
    !isWin ? join(home, '.local', 'share', 'moli', 'bin', 'moli') : undefined,
    !isWin ? join(home, '.local', 'share', 'moli', 'moli') : undefined,
    !isWin ? join(home, '.moli', 'bin', 'moli') : undefined,
  ].filter(candidate => typeof candidate === 'string' && candidate.length > 0);

  const discovered = [];
  if (isWin) {
    const root = process.env.LOCALAPPDATA === undefined ? undefined : join(process.env.LOCALAPPDATA, 'Moli');
    if (root !== undefined && existsSync(root)) {
      let entries = [];
      try {
        entries = readdirSync(root, { recursive: true, withFileTypes: true });
      } catch {
        entries = [];
      }
      for (const entry of entries) {
        if (entry.isFile() && entry.name.toLowerCase() === 'moli.exe') {
          discovered.push(join(entry.parentPath ?? root, entry.name));
        }
      }
    }
  } else {
    const seen = new Set(listed);
    for (const dir of String(process.env.PATH ?? '').split(':')) {
      if (dir === '') continue;
      const candidate = join(dir, 'moli');
      if (existsSync(candidate) && !seen.has(candidate)) discovered.push(candidate);
    }
  }
  return [...listed, ...discovered];
}

/**
 * Locate the installed `moli.exe`.
 *
 * @param override - explicit path from configuration, when set.
 * @returns the absolute executable path, or undefined when nothing exists there.
 */
export function findMoli(override) {
  for (const candidate of moliCandidates(override)) {
    if (existsSync(candidate)) return candidate;
  }
  return undefined;
}

/**
 * Read moli's version banner.
 *
 * @param exe - absolute path to `moli.exe`.
 * @returns the version string, or undefined when the call failed.
 */
export function moliVersion(exe) {
  // Via runOnce, not a pipe: the sandbox blocks inherited-pipe capture, which
  // would report "unknown" even for a perfectly good executable.
  const outcome = runOnce({ exe, args: ['--version'] });
  if (outcome.status !== 0) return undefined;
  const text = outcome.stdout.toString('utf8').trim();
  return text === '' ? undefined : text;
}

/**
 * Normalize a diagnostic blob into one readable line.
 *
 * The engine writes "Error: ...\nReason: ..." to stderr; keep the leading lines
 * and drop control bytes so the message survives a JSON round trip.
 *
 * @param text - raw stderr text.
 * @returns the condensed message.
 */
function condense(text) {
  return String(text)
    .replace(/\u001b\[[0-9;]*m/gu, '')
    .replace(/\r/gu, '')
    .split('\n')
    .map(line => line.trim())
    .filter(line => line.length > 0)
    .slice(0, 6)
    .join(' | ');
}

/**
 * Decide whether a failure is the sandbox's Schannel block rather than a real
 * network fault, so the caller can say so explicitly instead of guessing.
 *
 * @param message - condensed stderr text.
 * @returns whether the low-integrity TLS restriction caused it.
 */
export function isSandboxTlsFailure(message) {
  return /SEC_E_NO_CREDENTIALS|schannel/iu.test(message);
}

/**
 * Classify a transport failure: did the host never answer, or did a wait condition
 * simply never become true?
 *
 * A blocked host fails at connect time (`Failed to connect`, reset, refused) or,
 * when the socket never opens, as a readiness timeout with nothing to show. A
 * readiness timeout can also mean a genuinely slow page, so that weaker case is
 * reported separately as {@link possiblyUnreachable}.
 *
 * **But not every readiness timeout is about the network.** The engine reports the
 * condition it was waiting for, and three of them mean the page was already there:
 *
 *     ... while waiting for a selector
 *     ... while waiting for a script to become truthy
 *     ... while waiting for a subresource response
 *
 * In those cases the document was fetched and parsed; what did not happen is the
 * selector appearing, the script becoming true, or the matching response arriving.
 * Telling the caller to retry or configure a proxy then sends them to look at their
 * network for a problem that is in their selector -- measured: `waitSelector` on an
 * element that is not on the page used to report "the host did not answer in time".
 * A timeout "while waiting for response headers" is the opposite case and stays
 * classified as possibly unreachable, because that one really is the server.
 *
 * @param message - condensed stderr text.
 * @returns `unreachable` (connect-time), `possiblyUnreachable` (network timeout), and
 *   `conditionTimedOut` (a wait that the page itself never satisfied).
 */
export function isUnreachableFailure(message) {
  const text = String(message);
  const connectFailure = /Failed to connect|Could not connect|Connection was reset|Connection refused/iu.test(text);
  const anyTimeout = /Timeout was reached|readiness timed out/iu.test(text);
  const conditionTimedOut = /readiness timed out .*?while waiting for (?:a selector|a script|a subresource response)/iu.test(text);
  return {
    unreachable: connectFailure,
    // A condition timeout is not evidence about the network: the page arrived. Only
    // the remaining timeouts are worth mentioning as a reachability possibility.
    possiblyUnreachable: connectFailure || (anyTimeout && !conditionTimedOut),
    conditionTimedOut,
  };
}

/**
 * Run one `moli` invocation and return its stdout as bytes plus its stderr as text.
 *
 * @param options - executable path, argv, timeout, and optional proxy.
 * @returns the settled outcome; never throws for a non-zero exit.
 */
export function runOnce(options) {
  const dir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'dsh-moli-'));
  const outPath = join(dir, 'stdout.bin');
  const errPath = join(dir, 'stderr.txt');
  let outFd;
  let errFd;
  try {
    outFd = openSync(outPath, 'w');
    errFd = openSync(errPath, 'w');
    const spawnArgs = [...options.args];
    if (options.timeoutMs !== undefined) spawnArgs.push('-t', String(options.timeoutMs));
    if (options.proxy !== undefined && options.proxy !== '') {
      spawnArgs.push('--http-proxy', options.proxy);
    }
    const result = spawnSync(options.exe, spawnArgs, {
      stdio: ['ignore', outFd, errFd],
      // Cancellation backstop, not the engine's readiness deadline: it must sit
      // above the `-t` value handed to moli, or the process is killed before it
      // can report its own timeout.
      timeout: options.spawnTimeoutMs ?? (options.timeoutMs === undefined ? 60000 : options.timeoutMs + 30000),
      windowsHide: true,
    });
    closeSync(outFd);
    outFd = undefined;
    closeSync(errFd);
    errFd = undefined;

    const stdout = existsSync(outPath) ? readFileSync(outPath) : Buffer.alloc(0);
    const stderrText = existsSync(errPath) ? readFileSync(errPath, 'utf8') : '';
    const failed = result.error !== undefined && result.error !== null;
    return {
      status: failed ? null : (result.status ?? 0),
      stdout,
      stderr: condense(stderrText),
      spawnError: failed ? `${result.error.code ?? 'spawn failed'}: ${result.error.message}` : undefined,
    };
  } finally {
    if (outFd !== undefined) closeSync(outFd);
    if (errFd !== undefined) closeSync(errFd);
    rmSync(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
  }
}

/**
 * Run one `moli fetch` and return its stdout as bytes plus its stderr as text.
 *
 * The timeout is spliced in *before* the caller's options. Appending it would
 * place `-t <ms>` after a trailing `--eval <expression>`, whose option there
 * swallows the value — so `moli … --eval "1+1" -t 30000` would evaluate the
 * timeout instead of the expression.
 *
 * @param options - executable path, argv tail, timeout, and optional proxy.
 * @returns the settled outcome; never throws for a non-zero exit.
 */
export function fetchOnce(options) {
  const prelude = options.timeoutMs === undefined ? [] : ['-t', String(options.timeoutMs)];
  const argv = options.args.length > 0 && options.args[0] === 'fetch'
    ? [options.args[0], ...prelude, ...options.args.slice(1)]
    : [...options.args, ...prelude];
  return runOnce({
    ...options,
    args: argv,
    timeoutMs: undefined,
    spawnTimeoutMs: options.timeoutMs === undefined ? undefined : options.timeoutMs + 30000,
  });
}

/**
 * Translate one tool argument set into the engine's argv.
 *
 * @param args - validated tool arguments.
 * @returns the argv tail (everything after the executable).
 */
/**
 * Build the `moli fetch` argument vector for one call.
 *
 * Exported so the mapping from tool parameters to engine flags can be asserted
 * directly. That matters more than it sounds: a parameter that silently fails to
 * reach the engine is indistinguishable from a feature that does not work, and the
 * only fast, deterministic way to tell them apart is to check the vector.
 *
 * @param args - tool arguments.
 * @returns the argv tail (without the executable).
 */
export function buildArgs(args) {
  if (args.dump !== undefined && !TEXT_DUMPS.has(args.dump) && !BINARY_DUMPS.has(args.dump)) {
    throw new Error(`unsupported dump: ${String(args.dump)}`);
  }
  if (args.wait !== undefined && args.wait !== '' && !WAIT_STAGES.has(args.wait)) {
    throw new Error(`unsupported wait stage: ${String(args.wait)}`);
  }
  const needsLayout = LAYOUT_DUMPS.has(args.dump) || args.layout === true || args.scrollbars === true;
  // The URL is caller input and goes LAST, after `--`. Without the separator a URL
  // beginning with `-` is read as an option: `moli fetch --https-proxy=...` answers
  // "unexpected argument", and a crafted value could set a flag the caller never
  // asked for. The engine says as much in its own error ("to pass '--not-a-flag' as
  // a value, use '-- --not-a-flag'"). Flags therefore have to be pushed first and the
  // positional argument appended at the end, which is why the URL is not argv[1].
  const argv = ['fetch'];

  if (args.dump !== undefined) argv.push('-d', args.dump);
  // Screenshots and PDFs silently produce nothing without the layout renderer.
  if (needsLayout) argv.push('--layout');
  if (args.scrollbars === true) argv.push('--scrollbars');
  // `scroll` and `selector` ride along in the same expression: the engine takes a
  // single `--eval`. `hasDump` matters -- see combineEval -- because with a dump the
  // expression exists only for its side effect, and without one it becomes the output.
  const evaluation = combineEval(args.eval, args.scroll, args.dump !== undefined, args.selector);
  if (evaluation !== undefined) argv.push('--eval', evaluation);
  if (args.wait !== undefined && args.wait !== '') argv.push('--wait', args.wait);
  if (args.waitSelector !== undefined && args.waitSelector !== '') argv.push('--wait-selector', args.waitSelector);
  if (args.waitScript !== undefined && args.waitScript !== '') argv.push('--wait-script', args.waitScript);
  // Response waits: the right way to await an AJAX list, where a fixed delay is a
  // guess. The engine takes one of each, and a caller supplying several is asking
  // for "any of these", which is the engine's own semantics for multiple waits.
  if (args.waitResponseUrl !== undefined && args.waitResponseUrl !== '') argv.push('--wait-response-url', args.waitResponseUrl);
  if (args.waitResponseJson !== undefined && args.waitResponseJson !== '') argv.push('--wait-response-json', args.waitResponseJson);
  // The engine's own switch, but only when the caller asked for a failure to be
  // surfaced: adding it unconditionally would turn every 404 into `ok: false` and
  // change what existing calls do.
  if (args.failOnHttpError === true) argv.push('--fail-with-body');
  if (args.delayMs !== undefined) argv.push('--delay-ms', String(args.delayMs));
  if (args.noJs === true) argv.push('--disable-js');
  if (args.noCss === true) argv.push('--disable-css');
  if (args.resources === true) argv.push('--resource');
  if (args.withFrames === true) argv.push('--with-frames');
  if (args.insecureTls === true) argv.push('--insecure-disable-tls-host-verification');
  if (args.userAgent !== undefined && args.userAgent !== '') argv.push('--user-agent', args.userAgent);
  if (args.profileDir !== undefined && args.profileDir !== '') argv.push('--profile-dir', args.profileDir);
  if (args.cookieFile !== undefined && args.cookieFile !== '') argv.push('--cookie-file', args.cookieFile);
  if (Array.isArray(args.headers)) {
    for (const header of args.headers) argv.push('-H', header);
  }
  return [...argv, '--', args.url];
}

/**
 * Execute one `moli fetch` request and materialize its result.
 *
 * Ordinary failures come back as `ok: false` values so the model can react; only
 * a malformed request throws.
 *
 * @param options - resolved executable, validated arguments, and output policy.
 * @returns the canonical tool value.
 */
export function runFetch(options) {
  // The configured no-verify default applies only when the call stays silent;
  // an explicit false still means "verify fully".
  const args = options.insecureTls === true && options.args.insecureTls === undefined
    ? { ...options.args, insecureTls: true }
    : options.args;
  // `selector` replaces the whole-page output, so combining it with either reader is a
  // call that cannot do what it says: one of the two would be silently ignored. That
  // is the failure mode this plugin keeps having to fix, so it is refused up front and
  // as a structured result, the same way a binary dump with no writeTo is.
  if (typeof args.selector === 'string' && args.selector.trim() !== '') {
    if (args.dump !== undefined) {
      return {
        ok: false,
        url: args.url,
        selector: args.selector,
        error: '`selector` and `dump` cannot be combined: a selector returns one container\'s text and a dump returns the whole page, so one of them could only be ignored',
        hint: 'Use `selector` to read part of the page, or `dump` to read all of it.',
      };
    }
    if (args.eval !== undefined && args.eval !== '') {
      return {
        ok: false,
        url: args.url,
        selector: args.selector,
        error: '`selector` and `eval` cannot be combined: only one expression value can be returned',
        hint: 'Put the extra work in `eval` and drop `selector`, or keep `selector` and read the text it returns.',
      };
    }
  }
  const argv = buildArgs(args);
  const timeoutMs = args.timeoutMs ?? 30000;
  const isBinary = BINARY_DUMPS.has(args.dump);

  // Reject a byte-returning dump with nowhere to put it before spending a fetch.
  if (isBinary && (args.writeTo === undefined || args.writeTo === '')) {
    return {
      ok: false,
      url: args.url,
      error: `dump "${String(args.dump)}" produces bytes and cannot be returned as text`,
      sandboxTlsBlock: false,
      hint: `Pass writeTo with an absolute .${args.dump === 'pdf' ? 'pdf' : 'png'} path, then read that file.`,
    };
  }

  const outcome = fetchOnce({
    exe: options.exe,
    args: argv,
    timeoutMs,
    proxy: options.proxy,
  });

  const bytes = outcome.stdout.length;
  const stderr = outcome.spawnError === undefined ? outcome.stderr : `${outcome.spawnError} | ${outcome.stderr}`;

  // Empty stdout on a zero exit is not a failure: a page can legitimately have
  // no content in the requested format, which is exactly what a client-rendered
  // page yields under `noJs` with a text dump. moli is right to print nothing
  // for it, and the old code answered with "moli exited with status 0 and no
  // output" plus a hint to re-check the install, sending the caller after a host
  // that was never broken.
  //
  // Both decisions live in this one branch on purpose. Splitting them -- empty
  // stdout treated as success here and stderr checked further down -- lets the
  // case below (silent stdout, a complaint on stderr, exit 0) fall through to
  // the normal success path with the complaint silently dropped.
  if (outcome.status === 0 && bytes === 0) {
    if (stderr !== '') {
      return {
        ok: false,
        url: args.url,
        error: stderr,
        sandboxTlsBlock: isSandboxTlsFailure(stderr),
        unreachable: false,
        possiblyUnreachable: false,
        hint: 'The engine exited cleanly but produced no output and explained why on stderr; the text above is its own message.',
      };
    }
    return {
      ok: true,
      url: args.url,
      kind: 'text',
      dump: args.dump ?? 'html',
      content: '',
      chars: 0,
      bytes: 0,
      empty: true,
      note: 'moli succeeded and produced no output, so the page had no content in this format. '
        + 'A page whose content is built by JavaScript yields nothing when noJs is set; '
        + 'the same URL renders normally without it.',
    };
  }

  // The engine signals an HTTP error with exit code 22 and, under
  // `--fail-with-body`, keeps whatever the output format produced. That is why the
  // body is still here: the caller is told the fetch failed *and* gets to read what
  // came back, which is what an error page is for.
  //
  // This branch is reached for binary dumps too -- a screenshot of an error page is
  // still a screenshot -- so it must not decode stdout as text.
  if (outcome.status === ENGINE_HTTP_ERROR_STATUS && bytes > 0) {
    // The status is in the stderr reason. A JSON dump also carries it in the body,
    // which is the fallback when the reason wording changes.
    const reported = httpStatusFrom(stderr);
    if (isBinary) {
      const failure = ensureWritable(args.writeTo);
      if (failure !== undefined) {
        return { ok: false, url: args.url, httpError: true, error: failure, hint: 'Pass an absolute path in an existing directory.' };
      }
      writeFileSync(args.writeTo, outcome.stdout);
      return {
        ok: false,
        url: args.url,
        kind: 'binary',
        dump: args.dump,
        path: args.writeTo,
        bytes,
        httpError: true,
        ...(reported === undefined ? {} : { status: reported }),
        error: stderr.trim() === '' ? 'the server answered with an HTTP error status' : stderr.trim(),
        hint: `The image the server returned was written to ${String(args.writeTo)}. Drop \`failOnHttpError\` to treat this as ordinary output.`,
      };
    }
    const text = outcome.stdout.toString('utf8');
    const status = reported
      ?? (args.dump === 'json' && text.trimStart().startsWith('{') ? parseStatus(text) : undefined);
    return {
      ok: false,
      url: args.url,
      httpError: true,
      ...(status === undefined ? {} : { status }),
      error: stderr.trim() === ''
        ? `the server answered with an HTTP error status${status === undefined ? '' : ` (${String(status)})`}`
        : stderr.trim(),
      content: text,
      chars: text.length,
      hint: 'The request reached a server and it refused. The content above is the error page as the engine rendered it, '
        + 'so it is often worth reading. Drop `failOnHttpError` to treat this as ordinary content instead.',
    };
  }

  if (outcome.status !== 0) {
    const sandboxTls = isSandboxTlsFailure(stderr);
    // A blocked host fails at connect time ("Failed to connect" / RST) or, when

      command: onWindows ? 'curl.exe' : 'curl',
